utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon to -- this is case number IT-04-81-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Could we have appearances for today, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everybody in and around the courtroom. Mark Harmon, Barney Thomas, Carmela Javier, and today we are joined for the first time by Inger de Ru for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Welcome Inger de Ru. Thank you so much. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Perisic is represented today by Mr. Gregor Guy-Smith, Novak Lukic, Chad Mair, Milos Androvic, Tina Drolec, and Daniela Tasic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Pursuant to Rule 15 bis, Judge David still indisposed. Good afternoon, sir. Did you have a good rest last night, are you well this morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continued] ... with my back last night. I have a herniated, disk but I feel better today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It looks like there's a cross line on the channels. We are hearing the French interpretation instead of the English interpreter operation. I'm on channel 4. Okay I'm told it's being attended to. Just to remind you, sir, that you are still bound by the declaration you made at the beginning of your testimony yesterday to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth. Remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I remember perfectly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And for the record, are we in closed session? May the Chamber please move into closed session. I thought we had to be in closed session for the witness to come in. Oh, okay, there's a screen behind.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Before I begin can I check, Your Honours, that all the necessary voice and image distortion is in place for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What do you want to check?

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Just that we are good to go on the image and voice distortions here. Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, we have another materiel list on the screen in front of us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want you, please, to look at the materiel that has been provided and take us through what those items are, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Under number 1, 7.62 millimetre round for an automatic and semi-automatic rifle and PM, machine-gun. A round 12.7 millimetre, then a shell, 60 millimetre shell impact, mortar shell, and 82 millimetre mortar shell impact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we just scroll across to the right on both documents in B/C/S, see that just under 2 million rounds have been provided on this occasion. Do you see that? Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I see that. That's in the first box. 1.997.525 rounds. The second box says 9.984; the third box, 192; and the fourth box, 1.535.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just so we can have some sort of image of that, is this a large shipment, what does 2 million rounds and 1500 mortar shells look like?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If we assume that a packaging of 7.62 ammunition, one case consists of 1.260 rounds or 1.120 rounds. They are different packaging. And we can, actually, if we take this figure, we can divide it by the number of rounds per case and then we can determine what the tonnage is. But this is a large delivery, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are we talking multiple truckloads?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Must be several.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, could we please tender that document as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be given Exhibit P583. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Mr. Registrar, can we please have 65 ter number 11064 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, sir, can you simply tell us the items that are being supplied?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Under 1, we have a mortar round, an 82 millimetre mortar round, and then a 60 millimetre mortar round. Then following that is a shell, a 90 millimetre shell for self-propelled gun, M-36.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. If that could please be tendered as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we see the quantities also. Can we scroll to the right, please. Thank you. They are admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P584, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Mr. Registrar, could we please have 65 ter number 01161 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you will see a reference to the General Staff of the VJ, and then in brackets "Kremna". I'm not sure that is a reference we've had so far. Can you explain what Kremna is a reference to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Kremna also appeared on the first list, and I don't know if it was also on the second list. It is a depot in Serbia. I think it's close to Uzice. I know because I drove by there, and I know that it's on the right-hand side of the road, the weapons depot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's in Serbia, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: He said so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could please tender that as an exhibit, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit P585. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. If we could please have 65 ter 00827 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, here I'm interested in the materiel that is being supplied. Could you help us with that, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Under 2, we see a 152 millimetre round for a Howitzer, D-20. Then below that we can see a contact-fuse round. Under that I can't see, and then up front it says rockets grad. That's higher above. I think that the JNA did not have these rockets. This is something that the Romanians or Hungarians had, but this -- these rockets were 128 millimetre calibre in the JNA with us. I cannot see the last box. I think it's some kind of shell because it says that it's a contact action shell. And also below that contact action or contact fuse round for M1, 155 millimetre; it's probably a Howitzer or a gun.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, could we just scroll across to see the quantities, please. And, Your Honours, if that could please be tendered as a Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit P586. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Mr. Registrar, could we please have 65 ter number 00782 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I am tardy. I apologise, but I have a comment. In the B/C/S under 12 there is nothing entered, and in the English version the word Paracin appears. If Mr. Thomas agrees with this comment of mine, we can remain at this number, but I just want to say this for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But it looks like what is written under 12 in the English version is an interpretation of what is written in B/C/S, military post MF04, I don't know what VPE stands for in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I think now we have a new document already. If we could just go back to the previous document, please. That's 827, 65 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... do you have any objection on this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. Yes, I don't have any objection to this document. To the previous one, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, Mr. -- finish with this onem, and then we can go back to the previous document, Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Thank you, that's what I was looking for.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, if you look, first of all, there's no name and address of sender, but do we see a reference to the place being Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We have military post 9170-54 Belgrade, that's a military post in Belgrade. That's on the left-hand side. This is filled by the person or organ issuing supplies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we scroll down, we can see the materiel that is being supplied which appears to be --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These are spare parts, I think. On top of the list it says RD which means spare parts, some small axles, glass and some elements.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Below that do we see a reference to a decision of the Chief of General Staff of the VJ?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you can just scroll it back to the left so I can read the whole thing. It says that it is issued pursuant to the decision - and then I couldn't see. Oh, yes - of the Chief of the Main Staff and then the number, confidential number of June 2nd, 1994.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's the Chief of the Main Staff of which army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Chief of the Main Staff, I think it's the Yugoslav Army, VJ. Although, the Yugoslav Army had a General Staff whereas the Republika Srpska army had a Main Staff. The VJ had the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, perhaps we can scroll across on the -- to the right of the B/C/S version so that we can be clear about this, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, it says of the Yugoslav Army, but the problem is it says Main Staff, whereas in Yugoslavia it was called the General Staff. And I think this is just printing error or typing error of the administrator who prepared this list.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, is the error in relation to the use of the term Main Staff, or is the error in relation to the use of the term VJ?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The use of the VJ in the -- points to this being the Yugoslav Army, but my only problem is that in the Republika Srpska army, they called it the Main Staff, whereas in the Yugoslav Army it was called the General Staff. The only problem is that these initials in B/C/S, GS, are a short form for General Staff, so you could interpret it as General Staff or as Main Staff in B/C/S, "general stab" or "glavni stab."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But in any event we know that the source was military post 917054 in Belgrade; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We also know that according to the B/C/S version it came from the General Staff of the VJ because GS stands for General Staff as you explained.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Well, it could stand for General Staff or Main Staff, glavni, general, or ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I thought you said GS stands for General Staff in B/C/S, so the mistake is only in the translation in the English version, but otherwise the original refers to the General Staff. Doesn't it do so, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right. GS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, just staying where we are at the moment, if you look up to the name and the address of the receiver, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: And if we can scroll across to the right on the English. Just pause. And upwards, please, Mr. Registrar. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We see the 30th personnel centre entered as the recipient.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the 30th Personnel Centre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The 30th Personnel Centre was the centre military post 3001 that handled officers and for awhile civilians, all their personnel files. Civilians who were employed in the former JNA, and who were on the payroll from -- on the payroll from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where were these personnels serving?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were serving in the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, if that document could please be tendered as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just have a question before this document is entered into evidence. In the 65 ter package for this document there were four pages. But according to me this is not a single document, so I would just like Mr. Thomas to explain whether he is only moving the first two pages to be entered into evidence, because as far as I could tell these four pages were four different documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: The document does comprise four pages, four lists of similar materiel. I wasn't intending to go through each of them. The details are similar, Your Honours, but I would want to tender the whole document, the whole exhibit into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, I would object because I think that it's a document that is not a single document. These are completely different documents. So if Mr. Thomas would like to tender all the documents, then I would like him to go through each document with the witness because I believe that they are not all -- not all the pages constitute a single document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: There's an objection, Mr. Thomas. Do you want to tender in documents that have not been seen by the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: I can rectify that, Your Honours. Before we tender this document, could we please go to the next page in each version, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, do we again see supplies to the 30th Personnel Centre. And if we scroll down we'll see reference to the materiel and also the order of the Chief of the General Staff of the VJ upon which the supply has been executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: If we could scroll down, please, Mr. Registrar, on both documents. And to the left on the -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It says here that these items are being issued at the request of the Chief of the General Staff. These are some articles, perhaps these are some barrels, are they barrels for artillery weapons or something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have checked, and these four documents are actually a single document, so I withdraw my objection because the fourth page is actually a summary of the previous three pages, so it's of a different format, and that's what confused me a little bit. So I withdraw my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Are you now tendering, Mr. Thomas?

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The documents are admitted. Can they please be given an exhibit number as one document of four pages.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours, this document shall be given Exhibit P587.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Thomas, Mr. Lukic has indicated that he has something to raise with the previous document. Would you like to go back to that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: I can do that, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: I think that was P586.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: And I accept, Your Honours, that there's no entry in the B/C/S in box 11 stating Paracin. That is something that appears in the English translation, and it would appear shouldn't be there. And on that basis, I'm prepared to accept that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's fine. Mr. Lukic, you had referred to box 12. You meant to say 11?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's column 11, and Mr. Thomas understood me correctly, so there are no more remarks or objections to the translation of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. And you are happy with it? Okay. Thank you. You may proceed, Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Mr. Registrar, could we please have 65 ter number 00957 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you will see that the receiver is the 30th Personnel Centre once again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What materiel is supplied to the 30th Personnel Centre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 7.62 bullet for an automatic or semi-automatic rifle, and it can also be used for a machine-gun, it's not written here, but it was the same type of bullet or round that was used for machine-guns.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many rounds?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you surprised to see the 30th Personnel Centre being named as a recipient for 350.000 rounds of ammunition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it's not clear to me in all of these lists that went through the 30th Personnel Centre, I'm not sure what this is about. Whether they had sent the ammunition papers to the 30th Personnel Centre, and then the 30th Personnel Centre subsequently issued fresh papers for individual units. Perhaps that is how it was done, but it is a little odd. I don't know whether it was a section in the -- that was part of the command that maintained some kind of administrative records. I really -- I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. If that could please be tendered as a Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. This will be Exhibit P588.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Mr. Registrar, if we could please have Exhibit number 00486 on the screen, please. That's 65 ter number 00486.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Once again, sir, do you see the 30th Personnel Centre as the receiver?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do we have 296.100 rounds of 7.9 millimetre ammunition on line 1?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And 270.000 rounds on line 2?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the entry on line 3?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It says Maljutka. It's an anti-armour rocket that was fired by an operator used for the destruction of tanks, armoured vehicles, bunkers, APCs and so on. Some Maljutka were also place d on armoured personnel carriers and choppers.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, if this document could please be tendered as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again, I would like to ask Mr. Thomas before you make your decision if this document has two pages, because in the 65 ter document, it seems that is these are identical pages in the B/C/S that are put together as one document, so in that case I would object. Perhaps we can place them on the ELMO if the Prosecutor intends to tender them just to make sure if these are completely identical documents. Just to check that it's not two materiel lists but only one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: I accept that it's only one, sir. I think the easiest way to deal with that is to simply tender page 1 of the exhibit that we have on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Thomas. Can we scroll both documents to the right, please. Sir, I notice that on the B/C/S version towards the very right end of the screen, there's a lot of handwritten markings there. Can you read that for us because I don't see it on the English side. Are you able to read that? I see 562.000 and then 200. I don't know. Can you read that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is most probably once the ammunition or the rounds were delivered pursuant to the materiel lists. It's possible that the quantities stated did not arrive, so the operator received this number. He added all the numbers up. This is for number 1. For Article 3 it should have been 46 Maljutkas, but it says minus 20, meaning that he didn't receive 46, but he received 20 less, so probably the person who was receiving the shipment counted them up. This is probably his note, the person who received the goods saying how many of the goods he received. And I think this number here, 576.000 is the sum of 296.100 and 270.900, and that's then what came out, less than 200.000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Page 1 of document 65 ter number 00486 shall be given Exhibit P589. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Mr. Registrar, can we please have 65 ter number 00881 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you will see the receiver as being VP 7469 Zvornik. Was that in Serbia --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that in Serbia or the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. If that document could please be produced as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be given Exhibit P590.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Mr. Registrar, could we please have 65 ter number 01182 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you will see an entry for the name and address of sender. Can you tell us what that is?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm not able to hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Military post 41, and then 0-00, place Vrdnik, that would be the depot, and the dispatcher is the main command Novi Sad, and then it also says military post Vrdnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where is Vrdnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Vrdnik is probably somewhere in Vojvodina near Novi Sad because I can see that the command is in Novi Sad, so it could be a small town or a village near Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Serbia or Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Serbia, specifically Vojvodina, the autonomous province of Vojvodina, which is normally part of Serbia. It says Novi Sad here at the top, we have it there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where we have been talking about Serb facilities as being the source of this materiel, just so that we are perfectly clear, which army would all of these Serb facilities be subordinated to or part of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the review of all these materiel lists, all these facilities and places were in the territory of Serbia under the jurisdiction of the Army of Yugoslavia, the VJ. Except for the maintenance repair depot in Kragujevac. I don't know if that was under the jurisdiction of the VJ, some of the firms were working such as Pretis Vogosca in their capacity as half civilian, half military facilities. So in that case I'm not quite sure. There were a lot of these maintenance and repair depots, and they mostly all worked for the army. But I don't know if they were directly subordinated to the General Staff or to the federal Secretariat for national defence, or perhaps they were directly subordinated to the chief of the General Staff, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those are the repair institutes you are talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, because the federal Secretariat for national defence is like the Ministry of Defence, something to that effect. So these maintenance and repair depots and military equipment producing firms, I don't know if they were subordinated to the Army of Yugoslavia or to the federal Secretariat. I don't know. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if I understand what you've told us, the only one of those we have referred to is Kragujevac; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but we have it here that it was issued pursuant to an order of the General Staff, and not on the basis of a request --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just pause.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... from the ministry or the federal Secretariat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just pause for a moment. The only repair institute that we have spoken about so far when we've been looking at these delivery -- these materiel sheets today and yesterday has been Kragujevac; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. The other facilities that we have seen as geographically located in Serbia were not repair institutes; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And those were subordinated to the VJ; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we look now at the document that is on our screen, if you look at the date at the top left and at the top right, we see that there is no date entered in that part of the document; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nevertheless, if we scroll down in the English version, just to there, and if you look at the reference to the order in the original version, do we see a reference there to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just wait for my question. Do we see a reference there to a decision of the General Staff dated 9/12/1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, if we could tender that document as an exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry. Finally just actually down where there has been a receipt signature, we see the date 14th of December, 1993; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. If we could please produce that document as a Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. This will be Exhibit P591.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't wish to state my objection until the end of this line of questioning, but in future I would ask that this whole line of questioning put by Mr. Thomas involved the witness only reading what he saw on the document. Mr. Thomas said there's no date, the witness confirmed. Mr. Thomas said can you read the date of the Chief of General Staff; he read it, and that's how the document was tendered. I think that this manner of questioning of this witness for this particular type of document is not really necessary. The witness is simply reading the document. I have nothing against questions such as where was such and such a place or location, and that kind of question, but in this case the witness really is just reading from the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: I accept my friend's comments, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Fine. Thank you so much. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could we please have 65 ter number 01183 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, can you just help us with the materiel that has been supplied on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On this occasion we had 7.62 millimetre rounds for automatic, semi-automatic, and machine-guns. This is under 1. Then we have 7.62 rounds for pistols and machine-guns. Then also we have a round for the PAT M55 tank, and then also PAT M53/59, this is probably also a 20 millimetre round for an anti-aircraft gun. We don't have anything in the top boxes. We only have the name of the VJ and also we have --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just pause.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the military post.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, that's fine. I only asked you about the materiel that's being supplied. Please just answer the questions I pose to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Could we please tender that document as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. This document becomes Exhibit P592.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Mr. Registrar, could we please have Exhibit 65 ter number 1181 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The details that we have been looking for so far appear on this document and require no further explanation, but I just wanted to ask you about box number 3 in this form where there's reference to a contract number. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could you scroll the -- contract number. Thank you. It's okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The box is empty in that box for the contract number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What would usually go in there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If there was a contract, then you would enter the contract number signed between the Kragujevac maintenance and repair depot, the unit, and the person who orders the equipment, so then you would have contract number such and such.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, if we could move to page 2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell us, please, what materiel is being supplied there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Under 1, 152 millimetre round contact fuse for the D20 Howitzer. And 130 millimetre round, it's a contact fuse shell for the 130 millimetre gun.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, if that document both pages could be tendered as an exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a problem. Perhaps we can scroll down the B/C/S and the English version so that we can look at box 36. In the B/C/S version it says materiel taken by Lakic Milorad, and I don't think that the same thing is said on the English and the B/C/S version because it says LPRM 5191, and I don't think the same thing is said in the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Well, I'm happy to MFI that document, sir. I couldn't comment. If my learned friend can suggest a way through for us, I can say that the Prosecution doesn't place reliance upon that particular notation, and I'm prepared to accept what my learned friend says is in the B/C/S version if that is sufficient for our purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Maybe I'm not just quite sharp, but I can't see this LPRM 5195 even on the B/C/S. Under box 36, you said, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the bottom of the first page, Your Honour, what it says in column down there, column 36, it says VSR, as I said, M, and so on and so forth. I assume -- and I can put this in the cross-examination. I assume that this is either the marking of the vehicle or something that has to do with the personal ID, but it's not a marking of the Army of Republika Srpska as it says in the English translation. Perhaps Mr. Thomas can freely clarify that with the witness. As far as I'm concerned, what it says in the English translation it seems to be a an abbreviation of the Vojska, the Army of Republika Srpska. That's what it looks like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, do you see on this page now it looks like the writing is identical. Is this the same writing? There's reference to M 5191. And in the B/C/S they say BCP, but then that side they say VSR, Army of Serbian Republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, all that is an abbreviation, but the VSR in English it says Army of the Serbian Republic. But this abbreviation does not stand because in B/C/S it would be VRS. So I assume that the explanation given here by the translator, that this is actually an abbreviation for the Army of Republika Srpska is wrong. That is simply all that I'm trying to point out. The numbers are okay. That's not at issue. This handwriting is in the Cyrillic script, and it says in Cyrillic VSR.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We have heard that, how do you respond, Mr. Thomas?

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: I must say, my friend makes a compelling argument, I can't comment on it, though, sir. I think that's an exhibit we'll have to mark for identification and resolve finally one way or the other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Then we'll have it in and mark it for identification, please. Can we give it an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. This document shall be given Exhibit P593, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. And Mr. Registrar, could we please have 65 ter number 01188 on the screen, please. I think we will need page 2 in the B/C/S and page 3 in the English.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: It's on. Page 2 in the B/C/S and page 3 in the English.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, is the military post of the sender shown as 8236, and the place being Bogovadja?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Bogovadja.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The reference I want to take you to is down below the materiel supplied. We can see it in both versions as they appear on the screen. The very last line where there is reference to the decision of the Chief of Staff of the VJ, do you see that, dated 20th of September, 1995? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what that says and what it means.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just a moment, let me just focus on this and read the entire text. What it says here is that 100 millimetre rounds for a T-12 gun have been taken over, that's what it says there. And it also mentions pursuant to which order and on what date. And then at the bottom it says these items should be returned on the basis of the decision of the Chief of Staff -- Chief of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, if that document could please be tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a problem with the translation, Your Honour. Although the interpreters have just confirmed the same thing that was translated into English in the text. What the witness has said right now, I would like to read now in Serbian what he has said: "The items should be returned on the basis of the decision of the NGS VJ." According to me, this word as translated into English is not legally correct, but maybe we can leave this for later on. I think the word "razduzenje" has not been properly translated or interpreted as "returned" because "razduzenje" does not mean to return, it means -- and I have to explain the word. This means that a person who has an item now forwards that item or delivers it to someone else. So that is my understanding of this word. I think the interpretation and translation are wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You say it's not legally.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You say it's not legal [Previous translation continues] ... translation. Is it linguistically correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this is a specific term in our language, and I think that also in linguistics there is another word, not only in the legal sense. Because we have a word return -- we have a word for return which is "vratiti", but "razduzenje" is a totally different word, and it means something else. Both linguistically and legally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've just heard a suggestion here that the correct word in English would be liquidation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: In military terminology this means return equipment issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't think these are minor errors, and I think it's important, otherwise I wouldn't really have any comments or objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, I know you are listening to the B/C/S interpretation. The interpreter has told us what that word means in military terms in English. I don't want to get into a debate with you as to what the interpreter said. I note, however, that the person who translated this document here said "returned." And when the interpreter interpreted what the witness said, she also said "returned." Having said that, I ask you, Mr. Thomas, do you have any comment?

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Well, sir, I was going to move on to the next page in the same document which has the same problem at least so far as I can see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's deal with the problem first before you go to the next page, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: And I suggest that we mark this document for identification. We will get an official translation, and we can take it from there. I don't see a means of being able to resolve the conflict now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Are you at the stage of tendering, or you want to go to the second page?

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: We'll go to what would be the third page now, Your Honour, in the B/C/S and two pages further on in the English.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, sir, can you confirm that we have a similar reference in terms of action that is to be taken based on the decision of the Chief of General Staff in 22nd of September, 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you please scroll it up a bit. I can't see. The materiel list, if we can scroll it up. 032930 THE COURT: The English one, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: It would be on the next page of the English version, please, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the same issue as in the previous document.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Your Honours, could we tender, please, marked for identification pages 3 to 6 of the English and 2 to 3 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Those pages, 3 to 6 of the English and 2 to 3 of the B/C/S are admitted into evidence. May they please be given an exhibit number and marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. This document shall be given Exhibit P594, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Mr. Registrar, could we please have Exhibit 65 ter number 01189 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We see there a reference to military post, the receiver's military post as 7111, but the reference H. Pijesak. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is that a reference to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Han Pijesak was a barracks before the war. During the war, there was a barracks there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the formation of the VRS, who occupied those barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was used by the Drina Corps of the VRS, the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, if we could tender -- I'm sorry, if we could move on to -- sorry, Your Honours, if I could just have one moment quickly. If page 1 of that document could please be tendered as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Page 1 of this document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Page 1 of this document shall be given Exhibit P595. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And would that be a convenient moment, Mr. Thomas?

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: I was going to suggest, sir, there's one more of these left, and then we can finish open session and resume back in closed session after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How long will it take you to finish?

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Less than 2 minutes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Can we please have 65 ter number 01193 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see again, sir, that reference to VP 7111, Han Pijesak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And references to the facilities that you mentioned before in Serbia as the sender?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, if that could please be tendered as a Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's so admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P596.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We can break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're welcome. We'll take a break and come back at 4.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Could I confirm that we are in closed session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Just while the blinds are coming up, Your Honours, could we please have Exhibit 65 ter number 08234.01 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, what I want to show you first is a series of photographs of shell casings. To provide some context for you, these were taken from locations in the areas in and surrounding Srebrenica. The first document we have on the screen, do you recognise what -- the first photograph, do you recognise what we see there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I see a cartridge of 1.62 millimetres bullet. I see the manufacturer and the year of manufacture. It's PPU meaning the Prvi Partizan of Uzice, and the year is 1993, that's the year of manufacture.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, could I just have a brief moment with Mr. Harmon, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: I just have an administrative question which Mr. Registrar might assist with me, Your Honours. I have four of these which I would want to tender, the only question is whether it's going to be simpler do that all at the end or individually one at a time because they all bear the same 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may, this can be all one Exhibit number, all four photos or five.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Can we turn then to page 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before we turn to page 2, how do we see that is a 1.62 millimetre thing? I didn't see this 1.62. Sorry, we have now moved.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a smaller cartridge. It's probably an automatic rifle, 7.62 millimetres bullet, and the date of manufacture is new. The other 7.9 millimetre ammunition was not of recent manufacture. There were quite a lot of stocks or supplies of that particular ammunition, and it was used for machine-guns, M53 which were a bit outdated, so we didn't really use that much of that type of ammunition. Most ammunition that was used was 7.6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If we could move to page 2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, sir, can you help us with what we see there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Same as before, Prvi Partizan of Uzice. The year of manufacture is 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: If we could move to page 3, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, can you comment on this cartridge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can see here that the year of manufacture is 1984 [as interpreted], from what I can see, and we have the number 10. It's some sort of code. I don't know if this is some kind of foreign manufactured ammunition or perhaps one of our factories produced it without any marks of the manufacturer, but only used a code, so on the basis of that code you could tell who the manufacturer was. But from my knowledge of domestically manufactured ammunition from the former Yugoslavia, you would have Igman, Konjic, Prvi Partizan Uzice; these were -- Titova Vogosca, Slavko Rodic, Bugojno, all of these were special purpose industries manufacturing the bullets. There is no such marking here. We only see 10 and 1994, so I don't know who the manufacture is.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, if we could move to page 4, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a little difficult to make out. Can you make out the markings on this casing? And if you can, tell us what you see.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the top, I can see number 24, that's what it looks like in the upper corner. At the bottom it's not clear, so I really cannot tell what type it is. I don't want to speculate. There is no marking. All I can see is number 24. I think that's what it says at the top.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever encountered --

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar, we don't need that image on the screen any longer. I can tender all four documents, Your Honour, please, as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I object, Your Honours, to tendering this entire document as evidence. The witness did not recognise two of these shells and for two he did provide specific information about the initials, but not much more about the calibre on the basis of which we could establish exactly what the Prosecutor is claiming. I suggest that we just mark this with an MFI number, and then the Prosecutor could try to bring this evidence in through a different witness so that we can then know precisely what it means or what it indicates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: I would accept that my learned friend has a valid objection in relation to the very last document that I showed the witness. I have no difficulty with page 4 being marked for identification. But in my submission, he was able to comment sufficiently on the first three for those to be tendered as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness gave the same comment about the third and the fourth document, but I still think that based on what the witness said we don't have a clear interpretation of the calibre in relation to documents 1 and 2. Other than PPU, and the year of manufacture would indicate a certain factor that it's Prvi Partizan Uzice and that the year of manufacture is 1994. But we still don't know exactly which calibre it is, and that poses a problem for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, can I suggest to you that whenever you reply, stay on the point you raised in the first place. You are now raising a new point which you hadn't raised in the first time. In the first place you were objecting to the last two. Now you are objecting to the first two on a different basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps the interpreters misunderstood, but my objection applies to the entire document. I'm sorry if the interpretation was wrong. It was a misunderstanding. I mentioned the same objection that in relation to the first two photographs, you can see certain indications which indicate something, but you still don't know what calibre it is. On the basis of what the witness said, I think that it is not enough for the Trial Chamber to accept on the basis of that that we are talking about 7.62 millimetre calibre. I have nothing against him explaining some concepts, but I don't agree that we are talking about 7.62 millimetre calibre here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure. But the shell itself doesn't show anything from which one can determine whether it's a 7.62 millimetre, but he has told us everything that he saw on it. And with respect to one, the first one, he ventured an opinion that it could be a 7.62 millimetre shell because of the size as he saw it, but he has told us everything that he read on that shell. What it is you want from him?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I understood is that he explained certain terms or certain markings that indicate certain concepts. I have no objection to that. But if this document is to be used as evidence that it is a 7.62 cartridge that we are talking about, this is what my objection is about because I believe that on the basis of what the witness said, we cannot take that as a fact. If we are talking about tendering this as evidence to indicate what certain things mean that are marked on this cartridge, I have no objection to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And your objection seems to be going to the weight to be given to that testimony of the witness relating to the exhibit, namely, is it a 7.62 shell.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Fine. That has nothing to do with admissibility; it's got to do with weight. Is that okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. The documents are admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document will be given Exhibit P599. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, are all four pages tendered or only the first two? Because Mr. Thomas agreed with my objection in reference to the last two pages of the document that the witness did not say anything that has to do with the origin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you want to say something to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: It was the last one, sir. It was my position that he sufficiently commented on 1 to 3, but not on 4. I have no difficulty with 4, page 4 being marked for identification and being given a separate number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So you are not in agreement, Mr. Lukic? You are talking of two pages. Mr. Thomas is talking of one page, page 4 only, which he agrees with you on. For the record, are you nodding to say you agree with him?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. The witness explained about documents 3 and 4. His explanation was the same that he sees these numbers, but he doesn't know the origin of the ammunition on the basis of those numbers. And he gave the same assessment for documents 3 and 4. And that is why my objection is identical. I don't see why Mr. Thomas would agree with number 4 and not agree with number 3, but I stand by my objection for both documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Simply because those two have no writing that indicates origin. He can't speculate on that. The first two he could identify them as coming from some particular company because the initials of the company are there. But with respect to the other two, he read them, read what was there, and told us what he thought of what was there. If the first two didn't have PPU, he would not have been able to tell us they came from PPU. But he can only interpret what is before him. He can't then suck an answer from somewhere and say, I suspect it must come from such and such a company. He can't say that. So he is -- he has sufficiently interpreted the document before us according to the particulars on the document. Do you need him to do more than that and venture that speculation? We can ask him to speculate.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But then I see the problem now, Your Honours, how can we then bring or tender this evidence in through this witness? I could also read what it says on that document. I don't see how this witness can be the one through whom this evidence can be tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... can tell us the origin as to those two that you can think of.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assume some kind of expert. An expert of the Prosecution or any other kind of expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... on the paper to tell him the origin. What is he going to see on the picture to tell him the origin of the shells?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assume that on the basis of the number on the cartridge, he could determine the origin. This is what I'm thinking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you saying that the number tells us about the origin?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can just speculate. The number must mean something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Everybody is going to speculate. He speculated that the number --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May be a code for something. So do you want further speculation?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, I just believe that if the witness doesn't know anything about the document other than what he read of the document, he is not an appropriate witness through whom the document can be tendered. This is the gist of my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But the first two, he also described them according to what he read on those two. He offered nothing new in addition to what he read, and then he read what he read on the other two.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. If we have a witness when he reads something on the screen but has no interpretation of what is actually written there cannot be tendered as evidence. This is a procedural objection on my part. That's what I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The objection goes to weight, Mr. Lukic. It goes to weight, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your directions in Rule 21 are, in my opinion, directed at knowing which evidence can be tendered or brought in through which witness. If we do not stick to those directives, then it can be just a matter of weight, but I think the directions can also indicate the suitability of a witness in order to tender certain documents so that there can be a connection between the type of witness and the type of document that can be tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Can we mark page 3 and 4 for identification, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Page 3 and 4 of the Exhibit P599 will be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Mr. Registrar, could we please have 65 ter number 07098.06 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And again, sir, to give you some context this was materiel taken from Orahovac, an alleged killing site near Srebrenica. Now, please tell us if you need this photograph enlarged. That can be done. I want you to look at both the labels on the small white packages and also the printing on the outside of the wooden crate if that assists. Again what we are looking for is any markings which might indicate which facility manufactured this materiel, what the materiel is, and the year of manufacture and how you work that out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I just wanted to make a brief comment to the previous question to clarify whom this will be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we just deal first of all with the picture that is on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course. This is a 7.62 millimetre bullet from Prvi Partizan Uzice of 1994, series 03-07, and it says that on the crate and we have boxes inside, and they each contain 15 bullets. If the intention -- if they were intended for automatic rifles. If they were intended for semi-automatic rifles, then each box contained 30 bullets. These were manufactured by Prvi Partizan in Uzice. Ammunition for automatic, semi-automatic, and machine-guns. 7.62 millimetres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I just want to take that one step at a time. What is it that tells you that it was -- that it was manufactured at Prvi Partizan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: PPU is there meaning Prvi Partizan Uzice, and then we have 94, meaning manufactured in 1994. 03 indicates the series, and 07 can perhaps indicate the month. But in any case, we are talking about 1994 as the year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is there any information on the labels actually attached to the small white boxes that is of assistance in determining who manufactured and year of manufacture? And tell us if you need to zoom in on those labels.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, could you do that, please. We have the same thing. It says 15 pieces, 7.62 millimetres bullets with normal pieces, M67. And then we have NC-08 gun powder and BL means Milan Blagojevic Lucani, and that is the gun powder manufacturer. There is also the series of the gun powder, batch 91237, so this was specifically then the pack for automatic rifle. There was no difference in the actual ammunition, only that automatic rifles were loaded with 30 bullets which were in the two boxes, whereas semi-automatic rifles were loaded by using just one of the boxes, but the box contained 30 bullets. The bullets, as such, are the same.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you've explained this in the context of the label on the outside of the box, but what is the notation in the bottom left-hand corner of the label?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. PPU means Prvi Partizan Uzice, 9403, manufactured in 1994. 03 is the number of the series.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is a series? What is that a reference to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ammunition was manufactured in a number of series, the same type of gun powder, for example, was used, and then you would use one series with one type of gun powder. So one series would be produced with one particular type of gun powder, another series could be made with either different or the same type of gun powder. It could be stable or volatile, and all the gun powder was kept in the Nikinci depot. If a batch of gun powder came that was suspected of not being volatile, then that batch would be returned to the depot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where is Nikinci?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, if that photograph could please be tendered as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no objection to the testimony or the to tendering of this document. The only thing I would like to do is that Mr. Thomas would need to present evidence on the actual location of the bullets, where they were held. Just the fact that this witness has stated that is not something that would be acceptable as evidence, so we are hoping that Mr. Thomas would lead evidence on the place where the ammunition was stored.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Very well. I don't know whether Mr. Thomas is going to do that, but you have no objection to the admission. The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. This document shall be given Exhibit P600.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, have you also become familiar with markings on artillery pieces and artillery components?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, simply to provide you with context, the foundation will be led later through another witness. In respect of shell markings located in Sarajevo which bore references such as KB9307, and I'm talking in particular about components coming from 120-millimetre mortar shells, do you have any comment to make on the meaning of the marking KB9307?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: KB or KV? If this is in Cyrillic then it should read KV. And I think that's what it is. I think this is Cyrillic transcription. The B in the Latin script is the same as V in the Cyrillic script, and I think this is an indication for Valjevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Firstly, let me clarify. Yes, it would be a translation of a Cyrillic letters. Given that, can you tell us what they mean.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This means KV, Krusik Valjevo. What number did you say?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As an example, 9307.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That would mean produced in 1993 in July, the seventh month, that series, that batch. In any case, the first two digits would indicate the year of production.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, for example, KB9402 would be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know what KB would be, but I said what KV means.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So KV9402, for example, would be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, it would be Krusik Valjevo, produced in 1994, series or month, February. But what is really relevant is the first two digits, the year of production. The other numbers are not that important, what batch of gun powder it is or ... so this is really for experts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, during the course of your testimony, you've referred on a couple of occasions to Pretis Vogosca. Now, what was Pretis?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Can we get assistance with the curtains. Thank you so much. The matter stands adjourned to tomorrow at quarter past 2.00, Courtroom I. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 19th day of February 2009, at 2.15 p.m. 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.49 p.m.
